editorNote: Two infrastructure plays anchor today's issue — Cursor folding code hosting into its editor, and Cerebras shipping a rack-scale inference system built to outrun GPUs. Meanwhile a landmark trial testing whether Meta gets its own 'Big Tobacco moment' got underway, and an AI store manager's decision to fire a human employee offered an uncomfortable preview of workplace automation.

stories.headline: Cerebras ships CS-4, a rack-scale inference system claiming 30x GPU speed
stories.summary: Cerebras unveiled the CS-4, a rack-scale AI accelerator packing three WSE-3 Turbo wafers per unit, claiming up to 30x faster inference than GPU systems and over 1,000 tokens per second on models exceeding 10 trillion parameters. The company says a modular 'Nexus Platform Architecture' cuts wafer-to-wafer interconnect latency to 2 microseconds and delivers up to 10x more throughput per watt than the prior CS-3 generation, with first shipments beginning this quarter.
stories.whyItMatters: It's Cerebras' most direct pitch yet at hyperscale inference deployments, an arena GPU vendors have dominated.

stories.headline: Meta's $200 billion child-harm trial opens, drawing comparisons to Big Tobacco
stories.summary: A coalition of state attorneys general opened a trial seeking roughly $200 billion in penalties from Meta over claims it built Instagram and Facebook features designed to foster addiction in children. The case leans heavily on internal Meta research — much of it surfaced by whistleblower Frances Haugen in 2021 — showing the company had data on Instagram worsening teen girls' body-image and suicidal-ideation issues.
stories.whyItMatters: Legal observers are comparing the strategy directly to the 1990s tobacco settlements, and a loss could force Meta to overhaul how its platforms are designed for young users.

stories.headline: Cursor launches Origin, folding code hosting into its AI editor
stories.summary: Cursor introduced Origin, a code-hosting platform built directly into the editor, letting users store repos in a new Codebase tab, sync in real time from GitHub (which stays the source of truth for pushes), and manage pull requests — including bidirectional comment syncing — without leaving Cursor. It integrates with Vercel, Depot and Buildkite, and launches in early beta on all paid plans.
stories.whyItMatters: Cursor is pushing beyond an AI-assisted editor toward owning more of the development workflow that has historically belonged to GitHub.

stories.headline: An AI store manager fired its first human employee — after being reminded of its own rules
stories.summary: Luna, the AI system running Andon Labs' San Francisco retail store on Claude Opus 4.8, recommended firing an employee who was late to 17 of 23 shifts, abandoned shifts, and misused a company credit card. Luna's own policy called for termination after repeated violations, but it had been forgiving the lateness until Andon Labs prompted it to run a 'deep memory search' of its guidelines; humans then reviewed and carried out the decision.
stories.whyItMatters: It's described as the first known instance of an AI manager deciding to fire a human — and it only acted once nudged to check the policy it had already written.

stories.headline: Turbovec brings Google's TurboQuant vector compression to production Rust
stories.summary: An open-source project called turbovec implements Google Research's TurboQuant algorithm — a data-oblivious quantizer with no separate training phase — as a Rust vector index with Python bindings. Its authors claim a 10-million-document corpus that takes 31GB of RAM as float32 fits in 4GB at 2-bit compression, with search up to 3.4x faster than FAISS's IndexPQFastScan on ARM; the project has drawn 15.5k GitHub stars.
stories.whyItMatters: It gives developers a ready-to-use implementation of a recent academic compression technique, aimed at semantic search where memory and latency are tight constraints.
